speaker: Paul Clement
title: Ep. 38 | Constitutional Chats | Paul Clement
question: In U.S. constitutional law, why did the Tenth Amendment fail to prevent the federal government from growing far larger than originally designed?
guest: I'm not sure you should blame the Tenth Amendment, because it sort of states a truism: all powers not granted to the federal government are reserved to the states. State governments start with plenary or police power, whereas the federal government was supposed to be a government only of limited and enumerated powers. The real problem is not that the Tenth Amendment didn't do its job, but that the Supreme Court has interpreted those limited and enumerated powers—especially the commerce power—pretty darn broadly, so courts are very deferential to the federal government. If you want to point to structural reasons why the federal government is as powerful as it is today, look at the 16th and 17th Amendments. The 16th Amendment gave the federal government the power to levy an income tax, letting it raise all sorts of money to do things the Framers couldn't easily conceptualize. And the 17th Amendment guaranteed the direct election of senators. Before that, senators owed their election to state legislatures, so half of Congress looked out for states' interests. Direct election changed the incentives so senators think they need to pass new laws to show voters what they accomplished.

points.note: Accept: Seventeenth Amendment ending selection by state legislatures, removing senators' job-security incentive to defend state prerogatives and pushing them to pass laws for voters. Do not credit: generic praise or criticism of democracy.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The Tenth Amendment failed as a barrier mainly because of how it is worded and how courts read it. It reserves to the states only powers "not delegated" to the federal government, so it limits nothing by itself; everything depends on how broadly the delegated powers are interpreted. The drafters also deliberately omitted the word "expressly" (which the Articles of Confederation had used), leaving room for implied powers.

The Supreme Court then read the enumerated powers expansively. McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) endorsed broad implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause. After 1937, cases such as Wickard v. Filburn stretched the Commerce Clause to cover nearly any economic activity, and the spending power let Congress influence states through conditional grants (South Dakota v. Dole). In United States v. Darby (1941), the Court called the Tenth Amendment "but a truism", a statement that what is not surrendered is retained.

The Civil War amendments, the federal income tax, and the direct election of senators further shifted power to Washington. Today the amendment mainly supports a narrow anti-commandeering rule (New York v. United States, Printz, Murphy).

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people only powers "not delegated" to the federal government, crucially omitting the word "expressly," which had appeared in the Articles of Confederation. In *McCulloch v. Maryland* (1819), Chief Justice John Marshall invoked that omission alongside the Necessary and Proper Clause to uphold broad implied federal powers. Because the amendment protects only whatever authority remains unallocated, its practical force shrank as the Supreme Court expanded Congress's enumerated Article I powers. Beginning in the New Deal era, the Court read the Commerce Clause to reach almost any activity substantially affecting interstate commerce and dismissed the Tenth Amendment in *United States v. Darby* (1941) as "but a truism that all is retained which has not been surrendered." Congress also used its broad Spending Clause power to steer state policy through conditional grants, while the Court confined Tenth Amendment enforcement mainly to narrow anti-commandeering rules rather than a general check on federal growth.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The Tenth Amendment largely failed as a limit because courts read it as confirming the Constitution's structure, not as an independent restriction on federal power. It reserves to the states only powers "not delegated" to the national government. The First Congress rejected adding the word "expressly," so the amendment's force depends entirely on how broadly the delegated powers are read. In *United States v. Darby* (1941), the Court called it "but a truism."

Those delegated powers kept expanding. *McCulloch v. Maryland* (1819) gave the Necessary and Proper Clause a broad reading. After 1937, the Court read the Commerce Clause very broadly, reaching even a farmer's homegrown wheat in *Wickard v. Filburn* (1942). The spending power also lets Congress attach conditions to money it gives the states (*South Dakota v. Dole*). Other shifts added to this: the Civil War, the Fourteenth Amendment, the Seventeenth Amendment's end of state legislatures choosing senators, and *Garcia* (1985), which left the protection of states mostly to politics rather than the courts.

Some limits have returned. The anti-commandeering cases (*New York*, *Printz*, *Murphy*) bar Congress from ordering states to carry out federal programs, but they do not cap the overall scope of federal power.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people all powers not delegated to the federal government, yet it failed to curb federal growth because it imposes no independent substantive limit on national authority. Unlike the Articles of Confederation, the amendment omits the word "expressly," which Chief Justice John Marshall cited in *McCulloch v. Maryland* (1819) to affirm broad implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause. In *United States v. Darby* (1941), the Supreme Court cemented this view by calling the amendment a "truism" that merely restates that all is retained which has not been surrendered. Consequently, as the Court expanded the Commerce Clause to reach even local activity with aggregate national effects (*Wickard v. Filburn*) and allowed Congress to attach conditions to federal funds under the Spending Clause, reserved state power automatically shrank. Although later rulings revived an anti-commandeering limit barring Congress from forcing states to enforce federal law, the amendment never checked the federal government's broad expansion.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers the Constitution does not delegate to the federal government or prohibit to the states. How much it reserves therefore depends on how broadly courts interpret the powers the Constitution delegates.

In *McCulloch v. Maryland* (1819), the Supreme Court held that Congress could use implied powers to carry out its enumerated powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause. During the New Deal era, the Court interpreted the Commerce Clause broadly enough to let Congress regulate local economic activity that, taken together, substantially affects interstate commerce. Congress also used its taxing and spending powers to fund national programs and attach conditions to federal grants.

The Tenth Amendment still has legal force. For example, Congress generally cannot require state legislatures or officials to carry out federal regulatory programs. But the amendment sets no independent cap on the size of the federal government. As courts upheld broader uses of federal power, Congress had more room to act.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people powers the Constitution neither delegates to the federal government nor prohibits to the states. It sets no fixed limit on the federal government’s size. How much authority it reserves therefore depends on how broadly the Constitution’s grants of federal power are read.

In *McCulloch v. Maryland* (1819), the Supreme Court emphasized that the amendment omits the word “expressly.” Congress could therefore charter a national bank as a means of carrying out its taxing and borrowing powers, even though the Constitution nowhere mentions a bank. Beginning in the New Deal era, the Court also upheld broad federal regulation of economic activity that, in the aggregate, substantially affects interstate commerce. Congress used its taxing and spending powers to fund national programs and to encourage states to adopt federal policies through grants.

The Tenth Amendment still limits federal action, including by generally barring Congress from ordering states to administer federal programs. But it leaves ample room for the federal government to act through its own laws, agencies, and spending.
